chunks: Ibrahim ibn Mahziyar from al-Hasan from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Aban ibn Uthman from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who swore to slaughter his son, so he said, 'That is from the steps of Satan.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: There is no contradiction between these two narrations, because the first narration only obligated him to slaughter a sheep, as he made that a vow upon himself. And the second narration was an oath. And we clarified that there is no vow in a disobedience, and slaughtering the son is among the disobediences. And if that is the case, then the slaughter of the sheep was not obligatory either, and that occurred as a recommended act.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a man vows to slaughter his son?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of *Nudhur* (vows), specifically distinguishing between a vow to perform a sin (slaughtering a son) and its expiation. Shaykh al-Tusi and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan clarify that while the specific act of slaughtering the son is not obligatory because it is a major sin (*ma'siyah*), the vow itself remains valid, with slaughtering a sheep serving as a recommended (*mustahabb*) fulfillment rather than a strict obligation. This highlights the principle that vows of obedience are binding, while vows of disobedience are not enforced in their literal form but may carry recommended compensatory acts.
